keycloak-37429.issue: Inconsistent error handling: `verifySafeHtml` throws raw `RuntimeException` on I/O problems, while the surrounding plugin code (`verify()`) wraps failures in `MojoExecutionException`. A missing or unreadable English counterpart file (which is derived from a path rewrite, so it can easily not exist) will crash the Maven plugin with an unhandled RuntimeException instead of a proper build-plugin error message.

Fragile path derivation: The English file path is built with `replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties")`. The character class is greedy and matches any underscore-separated run, so a base file name containing underscores before the locale suffix (e.g. `reset_password_email_en.properties`) would have more than just the locale replaced, pointing at a non-existent English file and failing the build. Also, if the file being verified already lives under `resources` (not `resources-community`) and is not the `_en` file, the first replacement is a no-op and the derived path may be wrong.

Missing file in error message: When an anchor in a translation has no matching anchor in the English source, the message `"Didn't find anchor tag ... in original string"` does not include the key or the file path, unlike the other validation message. In a multi-file verification run this makes the offending property hard to locate.

Missing newline at EOF: The file lacks a trailing newline ("\ No newline at end of file"). While properties files tolerate this, some tools and diffs may concatenate the last line with subsequent content or produce noisy diffs on future edits. Adding a final newline is a minor but standard fix.

Missing newline at EOF: The file ends without a trailing newline ("\ No newline at end of file"). While properties files load fine without it, POSIX-style text files conventionally end with a newline, and some diff/tooling (and linters in the theme-verifier pipeline, if any) may flag or mishandle it. Adding a trailing newline keeps the resource consistent with other properties files.

Missing newline at EOF: The file lacks a trailing newline at end of file. While Java properties loading tolerates this, some text-processing tools and diffs behave poorly without it; adding a final newline is a minor consistency fix.

Wrong language content: The `totpStep1` value in the Lithuanian (`messages_lt.properties`) translation file was replaced with Italian text ("Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:"). Lithuanian users will see an Italian message in the otherwise Lithuanian UI. The original Lithuanian text (with the FreeOTP/Google Authenticator links) should be restored or a proper Lithuanian translation provided.

Wrong locale script: The replacement text for `totpStep1` is written in Traditional Chinese (e.g., 您的、手機、應用程式、應), but this file is `messages_zh_CN.properties`, the Simplified Chinese locale. Users of the zh_CN locale will see Traditional Chinese for this message while all surrounding messages remain Simplified, an inconsistent UI. The text should be converted to Simplified Chinese (e.g., 在您的手机上安装以下应用程序之一：).

sentry-95633.issue:
Python version compatibility: `queue.Queue.shutdown()` (called in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` and relied on via the
`except queue.ShutDown` handling in `OrderedQueueWorker.run`) only exists in Python 3.13+.
On earlier supported Python versions this raises AttributeError, so shutdown will fail
(caught and logged per-queue, but workers will never exit via this path and `join(timeout=5.0)`
will time out, leaving daemon threads spinning on `work_queue.get()` forever). Verify the
minimum Python version for this service, or implement shutdown with sentinel values /
`queue.Queue.unfinished_tasks` signaling instead.

Data loss on processing error: `OrderedQueueWorker.run` completes the offset in a `finally` block even when
`result_processor` raised, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`'s exception handler
also marks failed messages as complete. This means a message whose processing failed is
treated as done and its offset becomes committable — the message is permanently lost
(at-most-once delivery). This directly contradicts the class docstring "Only commits offsets
after successful processing". If at-most-once is intentional, the docstring should say so;
otherwise failed items should leave the offset outstanding so the partition is not committed
past them.

Possible Bug: `terminate()` sets `shutdown_event` but never joins `commit_thread`, unlike `close()`.
Since arroyo's `terminate()` is used for abrupt shutdown this may be acceptable, but the
commit thread can still be mid-`commit_function` when the process tears down, committing
offsets concurrently with shutdown. Also note `join()` delegates to `close()`, which
triggers a full graceful shutdown — confirm this matches the arroyo `ProcessingStrategy`
contract expected by the surrounding pipeline (join is normally a wait-only operation).

Flaky test assertion: In `test_stats_reporting`, immediately after submitting 10 items the test asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0`. Since the pool's worker threads run concurrently with the test thread, all items may already have been processed (and the queue drained) before `get_stats()` is called, making this assertion intermittently fail. The subsequent `total_items == 0` assertion after the completion event is safe, but the first one depends on scheduling. Consider asserting on cumulative processed counts or removing the racy check.

Flaky distribution assertion: `test_different_groups_distributed` asserts that 20 group keys hash to exactly all 3 queue indices (`len(queue_indices) == 3`). This depends on the hash distribution of the group keys; if `get_queue_for_group` uses Python's string hash (which is randomized per process by PYTHONHASHSEED), there is a small but nonzero chance that all 20 keys land on fewer than 3 queues, making the test flaky across runs. Using fixed keys with a known mapping, or asserting a weaker property (e.g., consistency rather than full coverage), would be more robust.

Resource leak on failure: In all the new `test_thread_queue_parallel_*` tests, `factory.shutdown()` is called after the assertions rather than in a `try/finally`. If any assertion fails (or the polling loop times out and the final assert raises), the worker threads and queue pool created by the factory are never shut down, which can leak threads and cause cascading failures/flakiness in subsequent tests in the same process. Wrap the test body in `try/finally` with `factory.shutdown()` in the `finally` block.

Flaky timing assertion: `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` asserts that no offsets were committed after the failed message. This is inherently timing-dependent: the commit path may run concurrently with processing, and on a slow/loaded CI machine a commit could land (or the loop could exit before the failure path fully settles), making the assertion flaky. Similarly, `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_commit` asserts `committed_offsets[test_partition] == 105` after only waiting for `total_items == 0` without confirming all 5 messages were processed, so a partial commit could be observed. Consider asserting on the final settled state with an explicit wait for processing completion (e.g., call_count) before checking committed offsets.

Private API usage: The Kafka integration test drives `StreamProcessor` via its private methods `processor._run_once()` and `processor._shutdown()`. These are not public API and may change without notice, breaking this test silently. If no public run/shutdown helper fits, consider documenting the reliance or using the public `run()`/`signal_shutdown()` path in a thread.

Swallowed cleanup exception: In the `finally` block of the Kafka integration test, `admin_client.delete_topics([test_topic])` failures are caught with a bare `except Exception: pass`. Topic deletion failure leaves the test topic behind in the shared Kafka cluster, potentially polluting other runs. At minimum log the exception so cleanup failures are diagnosable.

calcom-22532.issue: Overly broad update: The new call `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` updates `updatedAt` for every selected calendar under the credential, regardless of which calendar(s) the availability fetch actually covered. If this method is invoked for a specific calendar's availability (or when the cache was fresh and no fetch happened at all, since the call sits outside the `if` block), calendars that were not refreshed will still have their `updatedAt` bumped, making stale calendars appear freshly synced. Consider scoping the update to the calendar(s) actually fetched, or only updating when `fetchAvailability`/`setAvailabilityInCache` actually ran.

Hardcoded locale: The cache timestamp is formatted with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)` regardless of the user's locale, even though the component uses `useLocale()` for translations. Users in other locales will see dates formatted in US style. Consider deriving the locale from the i18n context.

Stale cache list: `deleteCacheMutation` shows a success toast but, unlike `disconnectMutation`, does not invalidate any tRPC queries (e.g. `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`). If the parent does not refresh via `onSuccess`, the dropdown will keep showing the old "cache last updated" status after the cache is deleted.

Possible authorization gap: The new `deleteCache` mutation accepts an arbitrary `credentialId` from the client and passes it to `deleteCacheHandler`. If the handler does not verify that the credential belongs to `ctx.user`, any authenticated user could delete another user's calendar cache by supplying a different credentialId (IDOR). The handler implementation is not part of this diff, so this may already be handled there, but the ownership check should be confirmed (or enforced in the procedure) before merging.

Unnecessary query: When `connectedCalendars` is empty, `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` is still called with an empty array. If the repository does not short-circuit on empty input, this issues a pointless DB/cache query on every request for users with no connected calendars. Consider skipping the call when `credentialIds.length === 0` (or verify the repository handles the empty case).

Portability Bug: `sed -i '' -E ...` is macOS/BSD syntax only. On Linux (GNU sed), `''` is treated as the
input file and the actual env file path becomes the backup suffix/content, so the
`GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` update silently fails or corrupts files when the script is run on a
Linux machine. Use a portable approach (e.g., detect sed flavor or use `sed -i.bak`).

Masked Failures: `cleanup` always calls `exit 0`, including on the failure paths (rate limit hit at the
rate-limit branch and failed URL extraction). In CI or scripted usage the script will
report success (exit code 0) even when no tunnel URL was obtained, so callers cannot
detect the failure. Failure paths should exit with a non-zero status.

Stale Log Reuse: When Tunnelmole is already running, the URL is read from `/tmp/tmole.log`, but the log is
only removed when this script starts a new session. If the previous session's log was
written by a different run (or the running tmole was started elsewhere), the extracted URL
may be stale or belong to a different tunnel, and the script will happily write the wrong
`GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` into the env file.

grafana-80329.issue: Misused log level: The new cleanup paths log routine per-batch progress (counts, full ID lists, and conditions) via `r.log.Error`, including an always-nil `"err"` field. These are normal, successful operations, so every cleanup cycle will emit error-level log spam on all instances, and dumping potentially thousands of IDs per batch makes the lines very large. These should be Debug/Info level and drop the nil `err` field.

Possible infinite loop: `untilDoneOrCancelled` loops until the batch callback reports zero affected rows. If `deleteByIDs` reports affected > 0 but the rows were not actually removed (e.g., a driver misreporting `RowsAffected`, or a delete racing with replication/soft-delete semantics), `fetchIDs` will keep returning the same IDs forever, spinning DB queries until the context is cancelled. The old single-statement version re-ran a fixed DELETE, which was self-terminating by construction. Consider bounding iterations or verifying progress differently. (Uncertain whether a realistic trigger exists in practice, but the impact is an unbounded query loop in a background job.)

Possible Debug Change: The cleanup ticker interval is reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute. If this is a leftover debugging/testing tweak rather than an intentional change, running the cleanup job 10x more frequently could add unnecessary database load, especially since the PR's stated goal is to reduce lock contention during cleanup. Worth confirming this frequency change is intended for production.

sentry-80168.issue: Silent duplicate handling: The old code explicitly logged an error when two results shared the same group key and skipped the duplicate. The new dict-based approach (`results[result.group_key] = result`) silently overwrites the earlier result with no logging or metric, so the "this shouldn't happen" condition the previous code guarded against can now occur invisibly. If duplicate group keys ever appear, occurrences will be dropped without any signal to investigate.

Test data mismatch: In `test_state_results_multi_group`, the packet sets `group_2` to 10, but the expected occurrence is built via `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(..., "group_2", 6, ...)`, using the wrong value (6 instead of 10). The same pattern appears in `test_results_on_change` and `test_dedupe` in `TestEvaluate`, where the packet values are 100 and 8 but the expected occurrence is built with value 6. The tests currently pass only because the value doesn't affect the occurrence fields being compared (e.g., fingerprint), which makes the fixtures misleading and fragile if occurrence construction ever incorporates the value.

sentry-80528.issue: Unused config copy: In `get_monitor_environment_context`, the code makes `config = monitor_environment.monitor.config.copy()` and converts `schedule_type` to its human-readable display value, but then returns the original `monitor_environment.monitor.config` in the `"config"` key. The copy and the `schedule_type` conversion are discarded, so the context still contains the raw enum/int `schedule_type` instead of the display value the conversion was clearly intended to provide. The returned dict should use the modified `config` copy.

Signal sent without occurrence: `monitor_environment_failed.send(...)` fires unconditionally at the end of the function, even when no occurrence was created because the incident is None (ERROR branch where `monitor_env.active_incident` is None) or because the monitor/environment is muted. Consumers of this signal (e.g., notification handlers) may therefore act on a failure for a muted monitor or one with no active incident. If this is intentional (signal means "status changed/failed check-in" rather than "occurrence created"), it should be documented; otherwise the signal should be gated on the same conditions as occurrence creation.

Ambiguous check-in ordering: In the threshold > 1 path, the query orders only by `-date_added` with no tiebreaker (e.g., `-id`). Multiple check-ins can share the same `date_added` (bulk check-ins for the same monitor are common), so the slice of the last `failure_issue_threshold` check-ins and the choice of `starting_checkin = previous_checkins[0]` (which sets the incident's `starting_checkin_id`/`starting_timestamp`) can be nondeterministic, potentially attributing the incident start to the wrong check-in.

grafana-76186.issue: Breaking interface change: Adding `FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger` to the `Logger` interface is a breaking change: every external or internal implementation of `Logger` (including test mocks/fakes) must now implement this method or fail to compile. If this is intentional for a major version, consider whether it belongs in a separate interface (e.g., `ContextLogger`) to preserve backward compatibility for existing implementers.

Fragile type assertion: `FromContext` type-asserts the result of `d.l.FromContext(ctx)` to `*log.ConcreteLogger` and silently falls back to `d.New()` when the assertion fails. If the infra logger ever returns a different concrete type (e.g., a value type, a wrapped logger, or a test double), the caller's context logger is silently discarded and replaced with a default logger, losing the intended log context (e.g., plugin ID / request-scoped fields) with no error or log signal. Consider logging a warning on the fallback path, or avoiding the assertion if the returned interface can be wrapped directly.

Lost log context: The removal of `pluginId`, `endpoint`, `uname`, `dsName`, `dsUID`, and `traceID` from the "Plugin Request Completed" log line significantly reduces the observability value of this log. This log is used for data-egress auditing ("grafana-data-egress"); without plugin ID, datasource name/UID, endpoint, or user login, it becomes hard to attribute a request to a specific plugin, datasource, or user. If this information is now expected to come from `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)` (contextual logging), that should be verified — otherwise this is a regression in audit/logging capability rather than a pure rename/chore.

Behavior change beyond rename: The PR is described as a rename, but it also removes the `instrumentContext` call (and the `instrumentContext` helper plus the `log` import), which previously enriched the request context with a contextual logger containing endpoint, pluginId, datasource name/UID, and user login. This silently drops those log attributes from all plugin requests passing through this middleware. If the removal is intentional (e.g., the logging moved to another middleware in this multi-file PR), it should be stated; otherwise plugin request logs lose plugin/datasource/user context.

grafana-103633.issue: Cache key collision: `userPermDenialCacheKey` builds keys by naive underscore concatenation, the same scheme as `userPermCacheKey`. Since `action`, `name`, and `parent` are free-form values that may themselves contain underscores, two different (action, name, parent) tuples can produce the same key (e.g. action="view", name="a_b", parent="c" vs action="view_a", name="b", parent="c"), causing a denial decision to be served for a different permission check. Consider a delimiter that cannot appear in these identifiers, or a structured/encoded key.

Ambiguous empty components: If `name` or `parent` is empty (plausible for namespace-scoped checks without a resource name), the key ends with consecutive underscores, which can collide with keys generated for non-empty values in edge cases and makes debugging cache entries ambiguous. Worth confirming callers always pass non-empty values or normalizing empty components.

Stale denial cache: The new `permDenialCache` caches a negative Check result for `shortCacheTTL`, but unlike `permCache` (whose entries are keyed the same way as existing invalidation paths), there is no visible invalidation mechanism for denial entries. When a user is subsequently granted the permission (e.g., an admin adds a role/permission), `Check` will keep returning `Allowed: false` from `permDenialCache.Get` before any permission lookup happens, so the grant does not take effect until the TTL expires. If the rest of the PR relies on cache invalidation on permission changes, that invalidation must also cover `permDenialCache` keys; otherwise this introduces a window where users are incorrectly denied access.

Denial cached on stale data: In `Check`, when `getCachedIdentityPermissions` succeeds but `checkPermission` returns `allowed == false`, the code falls through to `getIdentityPermissions` (DB fetch) and then caches the denial. That is fine, but note the denial is also cached when the DB fetch itself was triggered by a cache miss for an identity whose identifiers were just resolved — if `GetUserIdentifiers` creates/updates identifiers as a side effect or the user was just created, a race could cache a denial computed before the user's permissions exist. Lower severity, but worth confirming the intended behavior for newly created users.

grafana-79265.issue: Race condition: The limit enforcement in `CreateOrUpdateDevice` is a non-atomic check-then-act: it counts devices, and if under the limit, proceeds to insert. Two concurrent requests can both observe `count < deviceLimit` and both insert, exceeding the limit. Under concurrent anonymous traffic (the exact scenario a device limit targets), the limit can be silently exceeded. Consider enforcing the limit atomically (e.g., a transaction with a locking read, or a conditional insert based on the count).

Inconsistent time windows: The limit check in `CreateOrUpdateDevice` counts devices using `time.Now()` as the window reference, while `updateDevice` uses `device.UpdatedAt` as the reference for the 30-day window. If the incoming device's `UpdatedAt` differs from the server's current time (e.g., clock skew, or a client-supplied/backfilled timestamp), the two code paths evaluate different device sets: a device may be counted toward the limit yet not be updatable by `updateDevice` (its `updated_at` falls outside the window relative to `device.UpdatedAt`), causing `ErrDeviceLimitReached` even though the device exists. Using a consistent reference time (e.g., `time.Now()` in both) would avoid this.

Misleading error semantics: `updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` whenever `rowsAffected == 0`, but zero rows affected can also mean the device simply does not exist (or its `updated_at` is outside the window), not that the limit was reached. Callers distinguishing these cases (e.g., to log or return different errors to the user) will get a wrong signal. If conflating them is intentional, a comment or a distinct error/wrapping would make the contract clear.

Synchronous tagging on auth path: TagDevice was previously run in a background goroutine with a detached context and a 2-minute timeout, so failures or slowness never affected authentication. It is now called synchronously with the request context on every anonymous authentication. If the backing store (anonstore) is slow or unavailable, every anonymous request will block or fail on tagging, adding latency to the hot auth path. Consider whether the device-limit check needs to be inline, or whether tagging can remain async with only the limit check synchronous.

Request context for tagging: TagDevice now receives the request-scoped ctx instead of a detached context with its own timeout. If the client disconnects or the request is cancelled mid-authentication, tagging is aborted and the device may never be recorded, which could undercount devices and interact incorrectly with the new device-limit enforcement. The previous code deliberately used context.Background() with a timeout for this reason.

Behavior change: `TagDevice` now returns the error from `tagDeviceUI` instead of only logging it and returning nil. This changes the contract for all callers: a UI-tagging failure (previously treated as non-fatal) now propagates as an error. If any caller treats a returned error as a request failure (e.g., aborts login or middleware processing), previously-tolerated transient store errors will now surface to users. Verify callers handle this gracefully, or keep logging-and-continuing if the original intent was best-effort tagging.

calcom-22345.issue: Fragile SQL equality assertions: The tests now assert exact equality of `Prisma.sql` objects against hand-written SQL strings (e.g. `Prisma.sql`("userId" = ${...}) AND ("teamId" IS NULL)``). `Prisma.sql` equality depends on exact string fragments and parameter values, so any harmless whitespace or formatting difference in the service's query construction will fail these tests, making them brittle and tightly coupled to implementation text rather than behavior.

Lost type narrowing on teamId: The constructor now accepts `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions`, where `teamId` is optional and the union is no longer discriminated per scope. `buildTeamAuthorizationCondition` interpolates `options.teamId` directly into SQL (`"teamId" = ${options.teamId}`). If a caller constructs the service with `scope: "team"` but omits `teamId` (now allowed by the public type), the query binds `undefined`, which Prisma will reject or produce incorrect results. The previous zod-inferred `InsightsBookingServiceOptions` guaranteed `teamId` existed for the team scope; consider narrowing (e.g., asserting or re-validating scope "team" has teamId) before building the condition.

Array binding in ANY(): `Prisma.sql`("teamId" = ANY(${teamIds}))`` and the `userId = ANY(...)` variants pass a JS array as a single bound parameter. Depending on the Prisma version/driver, Postgres may fail to infer the array element type ("could not determine data type of parameter") or receive it as a non-array type, causing runtime errors. The commonly supported pattern is `Prisma.join(teamIds)` with `IN (...)`. This is uncertain (may work on some Prisma setups), but if it fails it breaks every org/team-scope insights query, so it should be verified with an actual query run.

Public API removed: The `findMany` method was removed and replaced by `getBaseConditions`, which now returns raw `Prisma.Sql` instead of executing a query. Any caller in the codebase that invoked `service.findMany({...})` will no longer compile, and callers must now manually attach the returned conditions to a raw query against `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized`. If other files in this PR migrate all call sites this is fine, but the migration must be complete since this is a breaking change to the service's contract.

calcom-10967.issue: Possible Bug: In `updateEvent`, the fallback branch is only reached when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, yet the new code searches `event.destinationCalendar` for an entry whose `externalId === externalCalendarId`. Since `externalCalendarId` is undefined/null here, the find can never match, so `selectedCalendar` is always undefined and the update is attempted with an undefined `calendarId`. Previously it correctly used `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. The same pattern is repeated in `deleteEvent` (`calendarId` becomes undefined), which will break updating/deleting events that rely on the destinationCalendar fallback.

Wrong calendar selected: In `createEvent` and `updateEvent`, `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is taken as the first entry of `destinationCalendar` without checking that it belongs to this Google credential (unlike `selectedCalendar`, which is matched by `credentialId`). With multiple destination calendars (the scenario this PR targets), the organizer email may be taken from a non-Google calendar's `externalId` (e.g., another provider's calendar ID), producing an invalid organizer email in the event payload.

Unused parameter: The new `externalId` parameter added to `createEvent` is never computed or derived inside the function - it is only echoed back in the returned result. If callers don't pass it (the parameter is optional), the result will always contain `externalId: undefined`, so any downstream logic relying on this new field (e.g., matching the destination calendar's externalId for multiple-host handling, per the PR title) will silently get `undefined`. Verify that all call sites actually pass this value, or derive it from `credential`/`calendar` inside the function.

Argument mismatch risk: `calendar.createEvent(calEvent, credential.id)` now passes the credential id as a second argument to the calendar adapter's `createEvent`. Without a referenced definition of the adapter interface, it's unclear whether all calendar implementations (Google, Outlook, etc.) accept this second parameter; adapters whose signature only takes `calEvent` would ignore it, while TypeScript may flag interface mismatches. Confirm the interface and all implementations were updated consistently in the other PR files.

Possible Bug: The old code used optional chaining (`evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`), so a missing destinationCalendar safely fell through to switching the location to Cal Video. The new code destructures `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` and then accesses `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining. When `evt.destinationCalendar` is undefined or an empty array, `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined` and this line throws a TypeError, crashing event creation for any booking without a destination calendar.

Possible Bug: In `updateAllCalendarEvents`, when a reference has a `credentialId` that is neither found in `this.calendarCredentials` nor resolvable from the DB (e.g., the credential was deleted, or `credentialFromDB.app?.slug` is falsy), `credential` remains `undefined` and `updateEvent(credential, ...)` is still called with it. Depending on `updateEvent`'s handling this either throws inside the loop (aborting updates for all remaining references) or fails silently for that calendar. The code should skip pushing the result (or record a failure result) when no credential could be resolved.

Silent failure: In `createAllCalendarEvents`, when a destination's `credentialId` cannot be resolved (not in `this.calendarCredentials` and the DB lookup fails or returns no app slug), the destination is silently skipped — no calendar event is created for it and no error is logged or surfaced. For a multi-host booking this means one host's calendar silently misses the event with no trace for debugging.

Type change ripple: The `destinationCalendar` property type changes from a single `DestinationCalendar | null` to an array `DestinationCalendar[] | null`. Any existing consumer of `CalendarEventClass` that reads or assigns `destinationCalendar` as a single object (e.g., `event.destinationCalendar.userId`, passing it to calendar APIs) will now be operating on an array and may fail at runtime or produce incorrect behavior. Since only this type change is visible in the diff, the actual impact depends on call sites not shown here; they should be verified to handle the array form.

Incomplete fix in recurring path: The PR converts the outer `bookingCalendarReference` lookup from `find` to `filter` to handle multiple calendar references (multiple hosts), but inside the recurring-event branch each `updBooking.references.find((ref) => ref.type.includes("_calendar"))` still only picks the first calendar reference. For a recurring booking with multiple hosts, only the first host's calendar event is deleted while the others remain, which is exactly the scenario this PR intends to fix. This inner lookup should also be a `filter` and iterate over all matching references.

Recurring path ignores reference credential: In the recurring branch, deletion iterates over all of the user's `_calendar` credentials rather than using the `credentialId` from the matched reference (which the code just resolved, including a DB fallback). If a user has multiple calendar credentials, events may be deleted from the wrong calendars or attempts made against calendars that never held the event. This behavior was carried over from the old code, but the PR's refactor to per-reference deletion makes the inconsistency more visible; the recurring path could resolve the calendar from `reference.credentialId` like the non-recurring path does.

Dropped select field: The rewritten `loadUsers` no longer selects `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` for dynamic-booking users. If downstream code in this handler (e.g., organization-aware dynamic link handling) reads `user.organization.slug`, it will now be undefined for dynamically booked users. Verify nothing consumes that field before removing it from the select.

Error handling regression: The new catch block in `loadUsers` converts the intentionally thrown validation errors (`dynamicUserList is not properly defined or empty.`, `eventType.hosts is not properly defined.`) into a generic 500 "Unable to load users", since plain `Error` is not an `HttpError` or `PrismaClientKnownRequestError`. These are client-input problems and should surface as 400 with the real message; the current code also hides the actual failure cause from logs.

Team calendars dropped: `teamDestinationCalendars` are collected and pushed onto `evt.destinationCalendar`, but the booking creation only connects `evt.destinationCalendar[0]` (the organizer/event-type calendar). Unless another code path (not visible in this diff) connects the remaining calendars, the collective members' destination calendars are silently discarded. Note: confidence is limited since handling may exist elsewhere in the PR, but within this file the extra entries appear unused.

Behavior Change: The condition for including `slug` in the organization create payload has been inverted: previously `slug` was included when `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED` was false (`...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })`), and now it is included only when `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED` is true. This is a semantic reversal, not just a style refactor. If the original logic was intentional (e.g., slug stored on the organization only in non-billing deployments), this change will alter organization creation behavior for billing-enabled or billing-disabled environments. Note the `metadata.requestedSlug` condition was NOT inverted (still gated on billing enabled), so the two conditions now diverge from their previous relationship. If this inversion is the intended fix, it should be covered by a test and the metadata condition reviewed for consistency.

Breaking interface change: The `Calendar.createEvent` signature now requires a second parameter `credentialId: number`, and `destinationCalendar` changed from a single object to an array. Both are breaking changes for every existing implementation of the `Calendar` interface and every caller that constructs a `CalendarEvent`. Since this is a type-only diff, the correctness depends on all implementations and call sites (not shown here) being updated in the same PR; if any adapter or caller is missed, TypeScript will surface it at compile time, but runtime behavior for loosely-typed callers could silently break (e.g., code still passing a single object as `destinationCalendar`).

calcom-10600.issue: Possible Bug: The field is registered with `methods.register("backupCode")` without a `required` validation rule. The HTML `required` attribute on the TextField does not enforce validation in react-hook-form — RHF relies on its own resolver/rules, so the form can be submitted with an empty `backupCode` value. Use `{...methods.register("backupCode", { required: true })}` (or a schema rule) to actually enforce the requirement.

Conflicting input props: `defaultValue=""` is passed alongside `{...methods.register("backupCode")}`. With react-hook-form, `defaultValue` should be supplied via the form's `defaultValues` option; passing it directly on a registered input can cause the field to be reset to an empty string on re-renders or when `reset()` is called, clobbering user input. Also, `minLength`/`maxLength` are raw HTML attributes that only constrain typing, not RHF validation — a value of the wrong length can still be submitted unless validation rules are added to `register`.

Possible Bug: `TwoFactorAuthAPI.disable(password, totpCode, backupCode)` is now always called with all three values, including when the user is in the normal TOTP flow where `backupCode` is empty/unset. If the server-side endpoint treats a present-but-empty `backupCode` differently from an omitted one (e.g., attempting backup-code validation and returning `IncorrectBackupCode`/`MissingBackupCodes` instead of validating the TOTP code), the standard disable flow could break. Consider sending `backupCode` only in the lost-access path, or confirm the API ignores empty values.

Possible Bug: Previously, `onEnable()` was called immediately after a successful TOTP verification. Now it is only invoked from the "close" button on the DisplayBackupCodes step. If the user dismisses the dialog via the X button, backdrop click, or Escape (the `onOpenChange` path), `onEnable()` is never called and `resetState()` is not run, so the parent component is never notified that 2FA was enabled and stale state (step, password, backup codes) persists for the next open.

Possible Bug: The "download" button inside the `<a download ...>` has no `type="button"` and no `preventDefault()`. It sits inside the `<Form handleSubmit={handleEnable}>` wrapper, so a click can also submit the form (default button type is "submit"), re-running `handleEnable` with the stale/empty TOTP code and triggering an unwanted API call or error toast while downloading.

State not reset: `resetState()` clears password, error, and step, but not `backupCodes`, `backupCodesUrl`, `dataUri`, or `secret`. After closing and reopening the modal, the previous 2FA secret and backup codes remain in component state (and the object URL is never revoked on unmount), leaving sensitive material lingering in memory/UI state longer than necessary.

Unhandled JSON.parse: `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` can throw if the stored `backupCodes` value is corrupt, was written in a different format, or decryption yields garbage (e.g., key rotation). An exception here results in an unhandled 500 rather than a controlled error response, and the user cannot complete the flow. Wrap in try/catch and return a proper error (e.g., MissingBackupCodes/IncorrectBackupCode).

Non-constant-time comparison: The backup code is matched with `indexOf`, a non-constant-time string comparison. Timing side channels on secret comparison are a known concern for auth codes; consider a constant-time comparison (e.g., crypto.timingSafeEqual on hashed values). Severity is low in practice, but it is a standard hardening step for one-time codes.

Backup codes overwritten on re-setup: Every call to the setup endpoint regenerates and overwrites `backupCodes` in the database, even while `twoFactorEnabled` is being set back to `false`. If a user revisits the setup page (or the endpoint is called repeatedly), any previously issued backup codes that the user saved are silently invalidated and replaced with codes the user may never have seen (e.g., if they abandon setup after the response is lost). Consider only generating backup codes when 2FA is actually being enabled, or preserving existing unused codes.

Codes active before confirmation: Backup codes are persisted (encrypted) at setup time while `twoFactorEnabled` is set to `false`. If the login/enable endpoints accept backup codes without checking `twoFactorEnabled` or whether the user completed TOTP verification, codes become valid before the user has confirmed setup. This depends on the enable/login endpoints not shown here, so verify their checks; if they gate on `twoFactorEnabled`, this is a non-issue.

Possible Bug: The new `backupCode` field is added to `LoginValues` and set via `methods.setValue("backupCode", ...)`, but the form uses `zodResolver(formSchema)`. If `formSchema` (defined elsewhere) does not include a `backupCode` field, Zod's default behavior strips unknown keys from the parsed output, so the value may never reach the sign-in request and backup-code login would silently fail. Verify `formSchema` includes `backupCode` (and that the submit path sends it instead of `totpCode` when `twoFactorLostAccess` is true).

Unguarded JSON.parse: `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, ...))` is not wrapped in try/catch. If the stored `backupCodes` value is corrupted, was encrypted with a different/rotated key, or is not valid JSON (e.g., legacy or manually modified data), `JSON.parse` or the decryption will throw an unhandled exception inside `authorize`, surfacing as an internal server error on login instead of a controlled error code. A guarded parse with a fallback to `ErrorCode.MissingBackupCodes` would be safer.

Race condition on code consumption: The backup code is verified and then deleted via a read-modify-write (`indexOf` on the decrypted list, then a Prisma update that overwrites the whole list). Two concurrent logins using the same backup code can both pass the `indexOf` check before either update lands, allowing a single-use code to be consumed twice. Not a data-loss bug, but it weakens the single-use guarantee of backup codes; an atomic conditional update would close it.

No rate limiting on backup code check: The backup code comparison happens before any rate-limit check specific to this path (the existing rate limit earlier in `authorize` covers the initial password attempt). An attacker with a valid password can brute-force backup codes via repeated `backupCode` submissions, since failed attempts (`IncorrectBackupCode`) are not throttled or counted here.

Security: plaintext storage: The new `backupCodes` column is defined as plain `TEXT`, which suggests 2FA backup codes may be stored in plaintext in the database. Backup codes are one-time credentials equivalent to a second factor; if the database is compromised, they would be immediately usable. Best practice is to store only hashes of backup codes (like passwords). Note: this migration alone doesn't prove how the column is populated (application code elsewhere may hash before writing), so this may be a false alarm — but if the application writes raw codes, this is a significant security gap.

Security concern: The new `backupCodes` field is a single nullable `String` with no indication of hashing. If backup codes are stored in plaintext (e.g., as a JSON array or delimited string), a database leak would expose reusable 2FA bypass codes. Best practice is to store only hashed backup codes (e.g., a bcrypt/sha256 hash per code). This may be handled in application code not shown here, so confidence is limited, but the schema design alone permits plaintext storage of high-value credentials.

calcom-8087.issue: Breaking signature change: `getCalendar` is converted from a synchronous function to an async one (now returns a Promise). Every existing caller that used the returned `Calendar | null` synchronously will now receive a Promise instead, silently breaking type checks and runtime behavior (e.g., `getCalendar(credential).lib` would be undefined). All call sites must be updated to `await` the result; no test coverage is added for this change.

Await semantics assumption: `await appStore[...]` assumes each appStore entry is either a Promise (from a top-level dynamic `import()`) or a plain value. If the async refactor changed appStore entries to be lazy factory functions (e.g., `() => import(...)`), awaiting the function itself would not load the module and `calendarApp.lib` would be undefined, causing every calendar type to log "not implemented" and return null. Verify the shape of the appStore entries matches what is awaited here.

Type change to Promises: Each entry of `appStore` changed from a module namespace object to a `Promise<module>` (dynamic `import()`). Any consumer that accesses properties synchronously (e.g., `appStore.googlecalendar.someExport`) will now get `undefined` at runtime and TypeScript type errors, unless every call site in the PR was updated to `await` the promise. If any consumer of `appStore` was not updated, this breaks app loading at runtime. Verify all usages were migrated to the async form.

Unawaited async callback: Changing the `forEach` callback to `async` means the returned promises are not awaited by `forEach`, so the `try` block completes before any of the calendar deletions finish. Any rejection from `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` (or from `getCalendar`) becomes an unhandled promise rejection and will never be caught by the surrounding `try`/`catch`, so failures to delete calendar events are silently lost. Use `for...of` with `await` (or `Promise.all` over mapped promises) so errors propagate to the existing error handling.

Unhandled async in forEach: The callback passed to `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach` is now `async`, but `forEach` ignores the returned promise. As a result: (1) the enclosing `try` block cannot catch any rejection from `getCalendar`, `calendar.deleteEvent`, or `deleteMeeting`, so a failed calendar deletion is silently swallowed instead of being handled by the surrounding error handling; (2) the caller of `Reschedule` cannot know when (or whether) the deletions complete. A concrete trigger: if `getCalendar` or `deleteEvent` rejects for one booking ref, the error never reaches the `try`/`catch` around the loop. Consider `for...of` with `await`, or `Promise.all` over mapped promises.

Unawaited promise: In `getCalendarCredentials`, `getCalendar(credential)` is now asynchronous (this PR converts it to return a Promise), but the result is stored unawaited in the `calendar` field of each entry. While `getConnectedCalendars` in this file was updated to `await item.calendar`, any other consumer of the array returned by `getCalendarCredentials` that reads `calendar` directly (e.g., checks `if (!calendar)` or calls `calendar.someMethod()`) will now operate on a Promise object instead of a calendar instance, silently changing behavior. If `getCalendarCredentials` is exported and used elsewhere, those call sites need the same treatment.

Sequential loading: `getVideoAdapters` now awaits each `appStore` entry inside a sequential `for` loop, so dynamic imports for multiple credentials are loaded one after another instead of in parallel. This is on the hot path of `getBusyVideoTimes`, which previously fanned out availability checks concurrently. Consider `Promise.all` over the lookups (or at least be aware of the added latency when a booking has several video credentials). Low severity, but a real regression in latency introduced by this change.

Async callback in forEach: The callback passed to `.forEach()` is now `async` and awaits `getCalendar(credential)`. `forEach` does not wait for async callbacks, so the subsequent `deleteEvent` calls inside the loop are started without the calendar being reliably resolved, any rejection from `getCalendar` becomes an unhandled promise rejection, and the outer code proceeds without waiting for these deletions. Converting this loop to a `for...of` loop (as done for the similar block in the `else` branch below) would fix it.

Possible Bug: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` does not wait for the async callback: `forEach` ignores the returned promise, so the surrounding handler can complete (and the response be returned) before any `calendar?.deleteEvent` call finishes or fails. Any rejection from `deleteEvent` or `getCalendar` becomes an unhandled promise rejection, and calendar events may not actually be deleted before the booking reschedule response is sent. Use `for...of` with `await` (or `Promise.all` over a map) instead.
